name: Carmine
summary: A red color made from cochineal insects. Many halal consumers avoid it because it is insect-derived.
halalWhen: Only if a trusted halal authority accepts the specific source and process
haramWhen: Listed as carmine, cochineal, or carminic acid without trusted halal certification
whatToCheck: Ingredient names such as carmine or cochineal
saferAction: Avoid unless the product has reliable halal certification that specifically covers this color.
notes: A vegan label usually excludes carmine because it is insect-derived.

name: Lecithins
summary: Usually halal when made from soy, sunflower, or egg. It is still worth checking the source if it is not stated.
halalWhen: Declared as soy lecithin or sunflower lecithin
Suitable for vegetarians or vegans when no alcohol carrier is used
haramWhen: Processed with a non-halal alcohol carrier
Source is unclear and the product is doubtful
saferAction: Generally acceptable when plant-based; verify if the source is not shown.
notes: Vegan labeling helps identify plant-based lecithin but does not replace halal certification.

name: Agar
summary: A plant-like seaweed-derived gelling agent that is generally considered halal.
halalWhen: Used as plain agar from seaweed
No doubtful carriers or alcohol-based flavor systems are present
haramWhen: Combined with haram ingredients elsewhere in the product
whatToCheck: Halal certification for the finished product
saferAction: Usually fine, but still check the full product ingredients.
notes: Agar is often used as a vegetarian alternative to gelatin.

name: Guar gum
summary: A plant-derived thickener from guar beans, generally considered halal.
halalWhen: Used as plain plant-derived guar gum
haramWhen: The finished product contains other haram ingredients
saferAction: Usually acceptable as an additive; evaluate the full food product.
notes: Source concerns are usually low for E412.

name: Gelatin
summary: Gelatin is animal-derived, so its halal status depends on the animal source and slaughter method.
halalWhen: Made from fish and accepted by the relevant halal authority
haramWhen: Made from pork
Made from non-halal-slaughtered animals
Animal source is hidden or unclear
whatToCheck: Vegetarian alternatives such as agar or pectin
saferAction: Avoid if the source is not disclosed; choose halal-certified gelatin or a plant-based alternative.
notes: Do not assume gelatin is halal. Pork gelatin is haram.

name: Acetic acid esters of mono- and diglycerides
summary: Related to E471 and source-dependent because the fatty acid base may come from plant or animal sources.
halalWhen: Confirmed vegan with no alcohol concern
haramWhen: Base fatty acids come from pork or non-halal animal fat
Source is not disclosed
saferAction: Treat as source-dependent; verify before relying on it.
notes: The suffix letter does not make it automatically halal.

name: Lactic acid esters of mono- and diglycerides
summary: The fatty acid part can be plant or animal based, so source confirmation is needed.
halalWhen: Lactic acid is produced by acceptable fermentation
haramWhen: Fatty acids come from pork or non-halal animal sources
Source remains unclear
saferAction: Verify source or choose certified products.
notes: Lactic acid itself is usually not from milk, but the fatty acids still matter.

name: Citric acid esters of mono- and diglycerides
summary: Often plant-based in modern production, but still source-dependent because it is made from mono- and diglycerides.
haramWhen: Made from pork or non-halal animal fats
Source is unknown
saferAction: Use when plant-based or certified; verify if only the E-number is listed.
notes: A plant-based label helps but is not equal to a halal audit.

name: Tartaric acid esters of mono- and diglycerides
summary: The halal concern is mainly the fatty acid source used in the mono- and diglycerides.
halalWhen: Fatty acids are from plant oils
haramWhen: Fatty acids are from pork or non-halal animal sources
Source is hidden
saferAction: Verify the source before treating it as halal.
notes: Related E472 additives should be checked individually.

name: Mono- and diacetyl tartaric acid esters of mono- and diglycerides
summary: Common in bread, DATEM can be plant-based but depends on the source of the fatty acid ingredients.
halalWhen: Confirmed suitable for vegans with no doubtful processing aids
haramWhen: Made from pork or non-halal animal fats
No source information is available
saferAction: Prefer halal-certified bread products or ask the manufacturer.
notes: DATEM is not automatically haram, but it is not automatically halal either.

name: Mixed acetic and tartaric acid esters of mono- and diglycerides
summary: Source-dependent because the mono- and diglyceride base may be plant or animal derived.
haramWhen: Pork or non-halal animal fats are used
Source is unknown
saferAction: Verify source; avoid doubtful products if no information is available.
notes: It shares the same main source concern as E471.

name: Sucrose esters of fatty acids

haramWhen: Fatty acids come from pork or non-halal animals

saferAction: Use only when source is plant-based or certified halal.
notes: The word sucrose does not remove the fatty-acid source concern.
